title: Guru Arjan's martyrdom day
hookLine: in the June heat Sikhs hand out cold sweetened water to passers-by

lines: ICE AND STEEL DRUMS, THE NIGHT BEFORE.
TRAYS HELD OUT INTO THE TRAFFIC.
THE OTHER SIDE OF THE TABLE.
cards: The night before, somebody's garage fills up with bags of ice. Big steel drums get rinsed out with a hose.
There's a crate of milk, a sack of sugar, maybe a bottle of rose syrup, and a stack of paper cups as tall as a child.

By mid-morning there's a table at a busy corner, it's well over a hundred degrees, and a line of teenagers stands in the traffic with trays, waving cars down. On day sixty-four, you were the driver being handed a cup.
Today, step around to the other side of the table.

teach.h: CHHABEEL — FROM SABIL, A FREE FOUNTAIN.
teach.b: The stall is called a chhabeel.

The word is usually traced to the Arabic sabil, a public water fountain given as charity, the kind built in Muslim cities from Cairo to Istanbul; a free drink of water is honored on more than one path.
You already know whose day it is.

teach.h: GURU ARJAN'S DAY, IN THE HEAT.
teach.b: On days sixty-three and sixty-four you met Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, held in Lahore in the summer of 1606, the first Sikh shaheed, and the line he held to: your will is sweet.

Today isn't the story again; it's how the Sikh year keeps it. The anniversary falls in the hottest weeks, in May or June, depending on which calendar a gurdwara follows. Inside, there's kirtan of his hymns and an Ardas.
Outside, the chhabeel. Here's how one actually runs.

teach.h: KACHI LASSI, ICE AND BOTH HANDS.
teach.b: The drink is often kachi lassi: water with a little milk and sugar, sometimes rose syrup, poured over ice in those steel drums.
It's handed out with both hands, to anyone, without asking a name or a faith: truck drivers, police officers, schoolkids, strangers.
A good chhabeel ends up with more helpers than it planned, because people walking past stop to pour. Some run for an afternoon, some for a week. Notice who holds the trays: very often the young.

teach.h: A MEMORY HANDED ON AS A JOB.
teach.b: That's how a memory four hundred years old gets handed on.
Not as a lecture about cruelty, but as a job: standing in the heat, cooling someone else.

how: On and around the anniversary of Guru Arjan's martyrdom in June, Sikhs set up chhabeels, stalls handing out chilled sweetened drinks free to passers-by, alongside kirtan and prayers at the gurdwara.

games.q: you're pouring at a chhabeel. a driver slows down, looks at the table, and seems unsure whether it's meant for him. what do you do?
o: explain the story of Guru Arjan first, then serve him.
hand him a cup with both hands, no questions.
point him to the gurdwara down the road.
games.why: a chhabeel serves anyone who passes, without asking a name or a faith. the remembering is in the giving.

practice: If a glass of cool water is near, hold it, feel the cold in your hands, and take one slow sip; if not, just picture one.

Think of someone worn out, overheated, overworked today, a delivery driver, a coworker, someone at home, and picture handing them the glass, and their face as they take it. If you pray, you can remember Guru Arjan's calm.

wordCard.voice: Chhabeel. A stall of cold sweetened drinks given free to passers-by, remembering Guru Arjan, who was martyred in the heat.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: a stall where cool drinks are given away free.

carryVoice: Your line: cool water for anyone. No name asked, no faith asked. Day one hundred fifty, done.
